S001.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
S001.description: Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes.
examples: Makes mistakes in homework or tests by misreading questions or skipping important parts.
Frequently omits details or makes typos in work documents or reports.
Repeats mistakes in calculations or numerical work, such as switching signs or getting digits wrong.
Performs tasks incorrectly by missing important details in instructions.

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
examples: Starts homework or projects but fails to complete them, submitting unfinished work or missing deadlines.
When given multi-step instructions, follows only the first few steps and forgets the rest.
Starts cleaning or organizing but switches to another task midway, failing to finish.
Leaves almost completed work reports or paperwork unfinished, neglecting the final steps.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
examples: Easily distracted and stops working due to small noises or movements nearby.
Cannot concentrate because eyes keep wandering to the scenery outside the window or people passing by.
Starts daydreaming or gets sidetracked by sudden thoughts while working or studying.
Loses focus and listens in when hearing side conversations or TV sounds.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
examples: Forgets appointment times or meeting schedules, arriving late or missing them entirely.
Forgets to reply to received calls or messages for days.
Frequently incurs late fees because of missing deadlines for utility bills or credit card payments.
Forgets to take medication or leaves necessary items at home when going out.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
examples: Constantly shaking legs or twisting and squirming body while seated.
Spinning a pen or fiddling with nearby objects, unable to keep hands still.
Continually changing posture and feeling uncomfortable while sitting.
Constantly moving, such as tapping the desk with fingers or tapping feet on the floor.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
examples: Feels uncomfortable and restless as if something is squirming inside when sitting still.
Feels internally anxious and stifled in situations requiring prolonged sitting.
A sense of urgency and anxiety that one must keep moving or doing something.
Feels unable to endure staying still and must constantly be doing something.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
examples: Unable to engage in calm activities for long, such as reading quietly or drawing.
Cannot play quietly, often shouting or making loud noises during games or play.
Unable to stay quiet in quiet places like libraries or movie theaters, making noise.
Cannot endure and avoids quiet and calm activities like meditation or yoga.

S014.name: Constant_Activity
S014.description: Is often 'on the go', acting as if 'driven by a motor'.
examples: Constantly moving and active as if driven by a motor.
Starts another task immediately after finishing one, without resting for a moment.
Unable to stay still even on weekends or days off, constantly doing something.
Appears to others to be always busy and bustling about.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
examples: Cannot wait and cuts in line or gets impatient when standing in a queue.
Rushes or cuts in without waiting for their turn in games or board games.
Keeps checking the time or complaining when waiting for their turn at hospitals or public offices.
Fidgets, complains, or gets annoyed in situations where waiting for a turn is required.

S018.name: Interrupting_Intruding
S018.description: Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations, games, or activities).
examples: Butts into conversations of others where they have not been invited.
Joins in on others' work or games without permission or interferes.
Touches or uses other people's belongings or work without permission.
Keeps talking to and disturbing others when they are focusing on work or studying.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity that is inconsistent with developmental level, present in at least two settings, and associated with clinically significant functional impairment. In adults and older adults, it often presents as chronic disorganization, difficulty sustaining effort, inner restlessness, and impulsive decision-making more than overt disruptive behavior, and symptoms typically have been present since childhood even if they were never formally diagnosed. The course is usually chronic, with symptom expression and impact shifting across the lifespan in response to environmental demands, compensatory strategies, and comorbidities. It is distinguished from anxiety, mood, and personality disorders by the early onset, pervasive cognitive and behavioral regulation difficulties, and a characteristic response to structured supports and stimulant or non-stimulant pharmacotherapy.

patient.personality: He is a routine-oriented, quietly generous retiree who enjoys solitary, hands-on projects and teaching practical skills to others in a calm, steady manner.
patient.stressor: When Lazaro retired a little over two years ago, he lost the external structure and clear deadlines that his years as a craftsman had provided, and he tried to fill the time with gardening, woodworking, and volunteering at the senior center. Without the built-in rhythm of a workday, he began starting multiple leisure projects at once—carving, recipe writing, music listening—finding it surprisingly hard to settle into any of them quietly for more than brief periods, which contrasted with the patience he remembered having on the job. Over the following year and ten months, this restlessness began to intrude on his enjoyment of activities he values, such as interrupting his own woodworking to repeatedly get up, change music, or check on the garden, and making it difficult to sit through calm family gatherings or focused mentoring sessions without repeatedly shifting gears. When his wife and adult children gently commented that he seemed unable to simply sit and enjoy his hobbies or conversations without constantly breaking the flow, and he noticed frustration in his grandchildren during shared projects, he agreed to consult a psychiatrist to understand whether there was an underlying attention problem contributing to these changes.
patient.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to just sit and enjoy my hobbies quietly anymore—I’m always getting up and breaking the flow.”

S001.name: Detail_Inattention_Errors
S001.description: Often fails to give close attention to details or makes careless mistakes.
S001.manifestation: Since I stopped working, I’ve noticed that even with simple things like a birdhouse plan or a recipe, I’ll misread a measurement or skip a step and only catch it when something looks off, which is frustrating because I used to be so careful with that kind of detail on the job.

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
S002.manifestation: These days I’ll sit down in the garage to sand a piece of wood or at the table to plan out the vegetable beds, and after ten or fifteen minutes my mind just drifts off and I realize I’ve been staring into space instead of actually doing what I meant to do.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
S004.manifestation: I start all these little projects—a new shelf, a soup recipe, organizing old photo boxes—but I keep finding half-finished things around the house because I wander off to something else and then don’t get back to them for days, if at all.

S008.name: Distractibility
S008.description: Often easily distracted by extraneous stimuli (for older adolescents and adults, may include unrelated thoughts).
S008.manifestation: When I’m working at the bench or trying to read, the smallest thing—a song change, a car going by, wondering if I watered the tomatoes—pulls me away, and suddenly I’m up fussing with something else instead of staying with what I was doing.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
S009.manifestation: My wife teases me that if she doesn’t write it on the calendar and remind me twice, I’ll forget things like calling the plumber back, taking my pills, or even a dentist appointment, because they just slip right out of my head once I walk into another room.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
S010.manifestation: I notice that when I’m sitting in a chair, whether it’s at church or at the senior center, my foot is always bouncing, my fingers are drumming on the armrest, and I keep shifting around like I can’t quite get comfortable.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
S012.manifestation: Any time I’m expected to sit for a while—like during a long family dinner or a movie with the grandkids—I get this pent-up feeling in my body, like I just want to stand up, walk around, or go check on something, even though I know it’s not really necessary.

S013.name: Quiet_Activity_Difficulty
S013.description: Often unable to play or engage in leisure activities quietly.
S013.manifestation: Even when I put on some music and tell myself I’ll just sit quietly and listen or do a bit of slow whittling, I end up humming along, tapping, talking to my wife, or popping up to fiddle with the stereo because being completely quiet and still feels almost uncomfortable now.

S014.name: Constant_Activity
S014.description: Is often 'on the go', acting as if 'driven by a motor'.
S014.manifestation: My kids joke that I wear a groove in the floor because I’m always puttering from the kitchen to the garage to the backyard, starting one little task right after another instead of just sitting down and relaxing like most retired folks seem to do.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
S017.manifestation: At the senior center, when we’re taking turns in a game or waiting to share something in the woodworking group, I catch myself getting impatient, fidgeting and wanting to jump in before it’s my turn, even though I know I should just wait.

S018.name: Interrupting_Intruding
S018.description: Often interrupts or intrudes on others (e.g., butts into conversations, games, or activities).
S018.manifestation: I’ve noticed that during family conversations or when I’m showing my grandson how to use a tool, I’ll cut people off or talk over them with my own thought or correction before they’re finished, and then feel bad when I see I’ve stepped on what they were trying to say.
